meta.titre: Asymptotes of Rational Functions: vertical, horizontal, oblique and holes

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Pure Mathematics with Mechanics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A transport company in Douala models the cost per passenger of a minibus trip as a rational function of the number of passengers: as the bus fills, the cost per head falls but never reaches zero, while for one special value of the input the formula would divide by zero and break down. These two behaviours, a value that is approached but never reached and a value at which the formula explodes, are what asymptotes describe. At Advanced Level every paper asks you to find the asymptotes of a rational function and often to sketch its graph, so the method has to be quick: factorise, cancel, test the degrees, and check the sign on each side.

items: A polynomial of degree $n$ has highest power $x^n$, and a quadratic can be factorised using its roots.
A fraction is undefined when its denominator is zero.
Polynomial long division writes $P(x)=Q(x)\times(\text{quotient})+(\text{remainder})$ with the remainder of lower degree than $Q(x)$.
The sign of a product or quotient depends on the signs of its factors.

sections.titre: Vertical, horizontal and oblique asymptotes of rational functions
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Vertical asymptotes
Write the function as $f(x)=\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$ with all common factors cancelled. A vertical asymptote $x=a$ occurs where $Q(a)=0$ and $P(a)\neq0$; there $|f(x)|\to\infty$. If a factor cancels, the graph has a single missing point (a hole), not an asymptote. A curve never crosses a vertical asymptote, because $f$ is not defined there.

### Horizontal asymptotes
Compare the degrees of $P$ (degree $m$) and $Q$ (degree $n$). Dividing numerator and denominator by $x^n$ gives:

$$
\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}f(x)=\begin{cases}0 & m<n\\[2pt] \dfrac{a_m}{b_n} & m=n\\[4pt] \text{no finite limit} & m>n\end{cases} \tag{1}
$$

where $a_m$ and $b_n$ are the leading coefficients. So $y=0$ is the horizontal asymptote if $m<n$, and $y=a_m/b_n$ if $m=n$.

### Oblique asymptotes
If $m=n+1$, divide $P$ by $Q$:

$$
f(x)=ax+b+\frac{r(x)}{Q(x)},\qquad \deg r<\deg Q \tag{2}
$$

The fraction tends to 0 as $x\to\pm\infty$, so $y=ax+b$ is an oblique asymptote.

### Behaviour near the asymptotes
Near $x=a$, look at the sign of $f(x)$ just to the left and just to the right: it goes to $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ according to the signs of the factors, and may differ on the two sides. A curve can cross a horizontal or oblique asymptote at a finite value of $x$ (solve $f(x)=y_0$); what it cannot do is stay on the asymptote. To see on which side the curve approaches, study the sign of $f(x)-y_0$ for large $|x|$.

### Sketching
Mark the asymptotes as dotted lines, the intercepts ($x=0$ and $f(x)=0$), any crossing of the horizontal asymptote, then draw each branch using the signs found.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the numerator has degree exactly one more than the denominator.
variantes.contenu_markdown: For $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-x+3}{x-1}$, division gives $x^2-x+3=x(x-1)+3$, so $f(x)=x+\dfrac{3}{x-1}$. The vertical asymptote is $x=1$ and the oblique asymptote is $y=x$. The curve lies above the line when $x>1$ (the fraction is positive) and below it when $x<1$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: For a linear numerator over a linear denominator.
variantes.contenu_markdown: For $y=\dfrac{x+3}{x-1}=1+\dfrac{4}{x-1}$ the asymptotes are $x=1$ and $y=1$. The intercepts are $(0,-3)$ and $(-3,0)$. For $x>1$ the term $\dfrac4{x-1}$ is positive, so the branch is above $y=1$ and falls towards it; for $x<1$ the term is negative, so the branch is below $y=1$. The two branches lie in opposite corners formed by the asymptotes.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a factor of the denominator is also a factor of the numerator.
variantes.contenu_markdown: $\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}=\dfrac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=x+1$ for $x\neq1$. The graph is the line $y=x+1$ with the point $(1,2)$ removed: there is no asymptote at $x=1$. The hole's height is found by substituting $x=1$ into the cancelled form.

sections.enonce_markdown: Find the asymptotes of the curve $y=\dfrac{2x^2}{x^2-x-6}$, describe the behaviour of $y$ on each side of the vertical asymptotes, and find the point where the curve meets its horizontal asymptote.

etapes.action: Factorise the denominator and look for common factors.
etapes.justification: The numerator is $2x^2$ and $x^2-x-6=(x-3)(x+2)$; neither factor divides the numerator, so nothing cancels.
The denominator is zero at $x=3$ and $x=-2$, and the numerator is non-zero there ($18$ and $8$).
Numerator and denominator both have degree 2, so the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients, $\frac21$.
etapes.resultat_markdown:
$$
y\to2\ \text{as}\ x\to\pm\infty \tag{1}
$$

The horizontal asymptote is $y=2$.

etapes.action: Study the sign of $y$ just either side of each vertical asymptote.
etapes.justification: The numerator $2x^2$ is positive, so the sign of $y$ is the sign of $(x-3)(x+2)$.

etapes.action: Find where the curve meets $y=2$ and on which side it approaches.
etapes.justification: Solve $\frac{2x^2}{x^2-x-6}=2$, which gives $2x^2=2x^2-2x-12$. For large $|x|$, $y-2=\frac{2x+12}{x^2-x-6}$, which is positive for large positive $x$ and negative for $x<-6$.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $x=-6$, so the point is $(-6,\,2)$; check: $y=\dfrac{72}{36}=2$. The curve approaches $y=2$ from above as $x\to+\infty$ and from below as $x\to-\infty$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Vertical asymptotes $x=3$ and $x=-2$; horizontal asymptote $y=2$; the curve meets $y=2$ at $(-6,2)$. Near $x=3$, $y\to+\infty$ from the right and $-\infty$ from the left; near $x=-2$, $y\to-\infty$ from the right and $+\infty$ from the left.

items.erreur_markdown: Stating that $y=\dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}$ has a vertical asymptote at $x=1$ because the denominator is zero there.
items.pourquoi_faux: The numerator is also zero at $x=1$ and the factor $(x-1)$ cancels. The function does not blow up at $x=1$; it is simply undefined at that single point.
items.correction_markdown: $y=x+1$ for $x\ne1$: a straight line with a hole at $(1,2)$ and no asymptote.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving $y=1$ as the horizontal asymptote of $y=\dfrac{x^2+1}{x-1}$ (ratio of leading coefficients).
items.pourquoi_faux: The ratio rule applies only when the degrees are equal. Here the numerator has the higher degree, and $y$ grows without bound.
items.correction_markdown: Division gives $y=x+1+\dfrac{2}{x-1}$: vertical asymptote $x=1$ and **oblique** asymptote $y=x+1$.

items.erreur_markdown: "A curve can never cross its horizontal asymptote."
items.pourquoi_faux: The asymptote describes the behaviour as $x\to\pm\infty$. At finite $x$ the curve may cross it, as in $y=\frac{2x^2}{x^2-x-6}$, which meets $y=2$ at $x=-6$.
items.correction_markdown: Solve $f(x)=y_0$ to see whether and where the curve crosses; only a vertical asymptote can never be crossed.

items.erreur_markdown: For $y=\dfrac{1}{x-3}$, writing the vertical asymptote as $x=-3$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The denominator is zero when $x-3=0$, that is $x=3$. Taking the sign from the factor itself reverses the position.
items.correction_markdown: Set the factor equal to zero: $x-3=0\Rightarrow x=3$.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying $y\to+\infty$ on both sides of $x=3$ for $y=\dfrac{1}{x-3}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The factor $x-3$ is positive just to the right of 3 and negative just to the left, so $y$ changes sign across the asymptote.

items.enonce_markdown: Find all the asymptotes of $y=\dfrac{4}{x^2+x-6}$ and state whether $y\to+\infty$ or $-\infty$ as $x\to2$ from the right.
items.solution_markdown:
Factorise: $x^2+x-6=(x+3)(x-2)$. The numerator is the constant 4, so nothing cancels and the vertical asymptotes are **$x=-3$ and $x=2$**.

The numerator has degree 0 and the denominator degree 2, so $y\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$: horizontal asymptote **$y=0$**.

For $x$ just greater than 2, $(x+3)>0$ and $(x-2)>0$ (small), so the denominator is a small positive number and **$y\to+\infty$**.

items.enonce_markdown: Show that $y=\dfrac{x^2+3x-1}{x+1}$ can be written as $y=x+2-\dfrac{3}{x+1}$. Hence find its asymptotes and say whether the curve meets the oblique asymptote.
items.solution_markdown:
$(x+1)(x+2)=x^2+3x+2$, so $x^2+3x-1=(x+1)(x+2)-3$ and $y=x+2-\dfrac{3}{x+1}$.

The denominator vanishes at $x=-1$ where the numerator is $1-3-1=-3\ne0$: vertical asymptote **$x=-1$**. As $x\to\pm\infty$, $\dfrac3{x+1}\to0$, so the oblique asymptote is **$y=x+2$**.

The curve meets $y=x+2$ only if $\dfrac{3}{x+1}=0$, which is impossible. So it **never meets the oblique asymptote**: it lies below the line for $x>-1$ and above it for $x<-1$.

items.enonce_markdown:
Consider $y=\dfrac{x^2-4}{x^2-5x+6}$.

(a) Simplify the function and state the equation of each asymptote. (b) Find the coordinates of the point where the graph is undefined but which is not on an asymptote. (c) Find the intercepts with the axes and state whether the graph meets its horizontal asymptote.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $x^2-4=(x-2)(x+2)$ and $x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)$, so $y=\dfrac{x+2}{x-3}$ for $x\ne2$. Vertical asymptote **$x=3$** only; degrees are equal with leading coefficients 1 and 1, so the horizontal asymptote is **$y=1$**.

(b) At $x=2$ the factor cancels: $y=\dfrac{2+2}{2-3}=-4$, so there is a hole at **$(2,-4)$**.

(c) $x=0$ gives $y=-\dfrac{2}{3}$: **$\left(0,-\dfrac23\right)$**. $y=0$ gives $x=-2$: **$(-2,0)$** (the root $x=2$ of the numerator is the hole). The graph meets $y=1$ if $\dfrac{x+2}{x-3}=1$, that is $x+2=x-3$, which has no solution: it **does not meet** the horizontal asymptote.

items_markdown: Cancel common factors first; a vertical asymptote is at a zero of the denominator that remains, a cancelled zero gives a hole.
Horizontal asymptote: $y=0$ if $\deg P<\deg Q$, $y=\frac{\text{leading coeff. of }P}{\text{leading coeff. of }Q}$ if the degrees are equal, none if $\deg P>\deg Q$.
If $\deg P=\deg Q+1$, divide to get the oblique asymptote $y=ax+b$.
Check the sign of $f(x)$ on each side of a vertical asymptote; the infinities may have opposite signs.
A curve can cross a horizontal or oblique asymptote at a finite $x$ (solve $f(x)=y_0$), but never a vertical one.
